shots.sub: around seven...
...or eight o'clock,
Most of us treat it like a law of nature,
like seven days in a week
shots.spec: stamp:7 DAYS / WEEK|NATURAL CYCLE|EARTH & MOON ORBIT|green

shots.sub: or 24 hours in a day.
shots.spec: stamp:24 HOURS / DAY|SOLAR ROTATION|LAW OF PHYSICS|blue

shots.sub: And if you ask people why we do it this way,
they usually tell you the same story.
They say life used to be an endless, brutal grind
that our ancestors worked from
sunrise to sunset every day
just to survive,
and that the five -day work
shots.spec: split:ANCIENT MYTH|365 DAYS|BRUTAL GRIND ✕|red|MODERN MYTH|5 DAYS|PEAK PROGRESS ✓|green

shots.sub: week is the pinnacle of modern progress.
That is the official story.
shots.spec: stamp:THE OFFICIAL STORY|TEXTBOOK MYTH|WHAT WE WERE ALL TAUGHT|gold

shots.sub: There is just one problem with it.
When historians opened the tax ledgers,
parish calendars, and court records
of the pre-industrial world,
they found the exact opposite.
Harvard economist Juliet Shor
examined the work records
of 14th century English peasants.
These were people living under feudal lords
with no tractors,
no electricity,
and no labor laws.
shots.spec: stamp:NO LABOR LAWS ✕|14TH CENTURY|ZERO UNIONS • ZERO HR|red

shots.sub: And yet, in a typical year,
a medieval peasant
worked roughly 150 days,
shots.spec: stamp:150 DAYS / YEAR|14TH-CENTURY PEASANT|HALF THE YEAR OFF ✓|green

shots.sub: not 260 days like
shots.spec: split:MEDIEVAL PEASANT|150 DAYS|HALF YEAR FREE ✓|green|MODERN OFFICE|260 DAYS|+110 EXTRA DAYS ✕|red

shots.sub: a modern office worker, 150.
Between winter lulls, harvest pauses,
and over 100 parish feast days,
medieval laborers spent nearly half the year
not working for their lord at all.
Even on work days,
the day was broken up by long midday meals,
afternoon naps, and ale breaks.
So how did a species with power grids,
computers, and time-saving machines
end up locked inside a stricter schedule
than a 14th century peasant?
shots.spec: split:1350 PEASANT|150 DAYS|NAPS & FEASTS ✓|green|2026 OFFICE|260 DAYS|STRICTER CAGE ✕|red

shots.sub: To find out,
shots.spec: stamp:300-YEAR WAR|1700s TO 1938|THE BATTLE OVER HUMAN TIME|red

shots.sub: you have to trace a 300 -year war
over something you carry in your pocket every day.
The clock.
For almost all of human history,
people did not work by the hour.
They worked by the task.
shots.spec: stamp:WORK BY THE TASK ✓|NATURAL HUMAN RHYTHM|FINISH THE JOB = GO HOME|green

shots.sub: If you were a cobbler, a blacksmith,
or a weaver in the 1700s,
your rhythm was bursts of effort
followed by long stretches of rest.
You worked hard when an order came in,
or when the harvest was ripe.
And when the job was done, you stopped.
Across England and early America,
artisans even had a weekly tradition
that drove early business owners crazy.
They called it Saint Monday.
shots.spec: stamp:SAINT MONDAY|THE 3-DAY ARTISAN WEEKEND|1700s ENGLAND & AMERICA|green

shots.sub: Sunday was for church,
family, and the tavern,
which meant Monday was for recovering from Sunday.
Workshops stood half empty on Mondays.
Many weavers did not touch their looms
until Tuesday afternoon,
working late on Thursday and
Friday to finish their quota.
shots.spec: split:MON - TUE AM|OFF WORK|SAINT MONDAY ✓|green|TUE PM - FRI|4 DAYS|FINISH QUOTA ✓|gold

shots.sub: Time belonged to the person doing the work
until the steam engine changed the rules.
A hand loom can sit quiet on a Monday morning
without costing a penny.
A massive coal-powered factory cannot.
Every hour those iron machines stood cold
was money burning in the furnace.
As historian E .P.
shots.spec: stamp:1967 • E. P. THOMPSON|HISTORICAL STUDY|TIME, WORK-DISCIPLINE & INDUSTRIAL CAPITALISM|gold

shots.sub: Thompson documented in 1967,
the Industrial Revolution was not
just a revolution in machines.
It was a revolution in human discipline.
Factory owners needed human
bodies that behaved like gears,
showing up at the exact
same minute six days a week.
shots.spec: stamp:6 DAYS A WEEK|MONDAY TO SATURDAY|LOCKED TO THE STEAM WHISTLE|red

shots.sub: In many early textile mills,
workers were forbidden from carrying pocket watches.
Only the master clock on the factory wall
was allowed to tell the time,
and mill owners routinely slowed the clock down during the shift,
so workers stayed 30
shots.spec: scene:42_clock_tampering_30m.png+badge:BOSS SLOWS THE CLOCK = +30 MIN FREE LABOR!|red

shots.sub: minutes longer without knowing it.
shots.spec: stamp:+30 MINUTES STOLEN|RIGGED FACTORY CLOCKS|WORKERS STAYED LONGER WITHOUT KNOWING|red

shots.sub: Saint Monday was crushed with heavy fines.
Parish feast days were wiped off the calendar.
shots.spec: scene:44_feast_days_trashed.png+badge:100+ FEAST DAYS WIPED OFF THE CALENDAR ✕|red

shots.sub: By the 1850s,
shots.spec: stamp:1850s • NEW NORMAL|EUROPE & AMERICA|THE INDUSTRIAL WORK SCHEDULE|red

shots.sub: the new normal across Europe and America
was six full days a week, 12 hours a day,
shots.spec: split:6 FULL DAYS|MON - SAT|NO SAINT MONDAY ✕|red|12 HOURS / DAY|72 HRS / WK|DAWN TO DARK ✕|red

shots.sub: with only Sunday left to catch your breath.
People did not evolve toward working more.
They were forced into a six
shots.spec: scene:41_human_in_gears.png+badge:FORCED INTO A 6-DAY CAGE IN 1 GENERATION|red

shots.sub: -day cage in a single generation.
shots.spec: stamp:THE 6-DAY CAGE|72 HOURS A WEEK|BUILT IN A SINGLE GENERATION|red

shots.sub: So how did Saturday finally break
free from that six -day cage?
shots.spec: split:1850s CAGE|6 DAYS ON|ONLY SUNDAY OFF ✕|red|MODERN WEEKEND|5 DAYS ON|SATURDAY FREED ✓|green

shots.sub: Most textbooks give the credit
to one man, Henry Ford.
shots.spec: stamp:HENRY FORD|DETROIT AUTOMAKER|CREDITED WITH THE 5-DAY WEEK|gold

shots.sub: On September 25th, 1926,
Ford stunned the business world
by announcing that his workers
would now work only five days a week,
shots.spec: stamp:5 DAYS A WEEK|SATURDAY IS NOW FREE|FORD MOTOR COMPANY (1926)|green

shots.sub: Monday through Friday,
for the same six -dollar daily pay.
On the surface, it looked like extraordinary generosity.
The head of U .S. Steel warned
that giving workers two whole days off
would destroy the moral fabric of America.
Wait, stop right there.
Henry Ford was one of the
most ruthless efficiency obsessives in history.
He had a private security
force that spied on his workers
to make sure they were not slacking off.
He did not give away millions
of hours of labor out of kindness.
shots.spec: stamp:NOT OUT OF KINDNESS ✕|ZERO CHARITY|IT WAS PURE COLD MATH|red

shots.sub: He had discovered a fatal math
shots.spec: stamp:FATAL MATH PROBLEM|CAPITALISM PARADOX|MASS PRODUCTION vs. ZERO FREE TIME|gold

shots.sub: problem at the heart of capitalism.
shots.spec: split:PRODUCTION|10,000 CARS|CHURNING OUT FAST ✓|green|FREE TIME|0 HOURS|NOBODY CAN DRIVE ✕|red

shots.sub: By the mid -1920s,
Ford's assembly lines were churning out
Model T cars faster than ever.
His workers even earned enough to afford one.
There was just one catch.
Why would a man buy a family
car if he worked six days a week,
shots.spec: scene:23_exhausted_worker_bed_model_t.png+ring:1430,360,240,WHY BUY A CAR IF YOU WORK 6 DAYS?

shots.sub: collapsed into bed on Saturday night,
and spent his only day off in church on Sunday?
A worker who is always working
shots.spec: split:ALWAYS WORKING|6 DAYS / WK|NO TIME TO BUY ✕|red|WEEKEND SHOPPER|5 DAYS / WK|2 DAYS TO SPEND $ ✓|green

shots.sub: has no time to be a customer.
shots.spec: stamp:NO TIME TO BE A CUSTOMER|HENRY FORD'S REALIZATION|EXHAUSTED WORKERS DON'T BUY CARS|red

shots.sub: Listen to what Henry Ford
told World's Work magazine in 1926,
right after announcing the five-day week.
People who have more leisure must have more clothes.
They must have a greater variety of food.
They must have more transportation facilities.
This increased consumption will require
greater production than we now have.
Read that again.
Saturday was not given back so you could
sit under a tree like an ancient hunter -gatherer.
Saturday was invented so you
would have time to go shopping.
One day for rest on Sunday.
One day to spend your paycheck on Saturday.
And five days to earn it all back again.
shots.spec: scene:09_ref_office_clock_desk.png+badge:MON–FRI = 5 DAYS TO EARN IT BACK AGAIN|red

shots.sub: And here is the part of the
story almost nobody gets taught in school.
shots.spec: stamp:THE FORGOTTEN CHAPTER|1930 TO 1938|WHAT NOBODY TEACHES IN SCHOOL|gold

shots.sub: In the 1930s,
nobody believed the five -day 40 -hour week was the final destination.
shots.spec: scene:49_keynes_road_fork.png+badge:1930s: 40 HOURS WAS NOT THE END GOAL!|gold

shots.sub: Everybody thought it was just a temporary stop on the way down.
In 1930, economist John Maynard Keynes
shots.spec: stamp:1930 • J. M. KEYNES|CAMBRIDGE ECONOMIST|ECONOMIC POSSIBILITIES FOR OUR GRANDCHILDREN|gold

shots.sub: calculated that with technology advancing so fast,
his grandchildren would only need to work about 15
hours a week — maybe three hours a day.
shots.spec: stamp:15 HOURS / WEEK|3 HOURS A DAY|KEYNES'S 100-YEAR PREDICTION|green

shots.sub: And in April 1933,
shots.spec: stamp:APRIL 1933|HEIGHT OF THE GREAT DEPRESSION|WASHINGTON, D.C.|gold

shots.sub: at the height of the Great Depression,
the U .S. Senate actually voted on
a bill introduced by Senator Hugo Black.
The bill made it illegal for any factory
or business to employ someone for more than
30 hours a week,
shots.spec: stamp:30 HOURS A WEEK|6 HOURS A DAY • 5 DAYS A WEEK|U.S. SENATE BILL (APRIL 1933)|green

shots.sub: six hours a day, five days a week.
shots.spec: split:OLD STANDARD|40 HOURS|8 HRS / DAY|gold|1933 SENATE BILL|30 HOURS|6 HRS / DAY ✓|green

shots.sub: And it passed the U .S. Senate,

shots.spec: split:U.S. SENATE YES|53 VOTES|PASSED THE SENATE ✓|green|U.S. SENATE NO|30 VOTES|DEFEATED|red

shots.sub: Kellogg's even switched its battle creek plant to
six -hour shifts and found that accidents dropped,
efficiency rose,
and workers had the entire afternoon free.
For a few months in 1933,
the six -hour workday was on the verge of becoming the law of the land.
shots.spec: stamp:SPRING 1933|ON THE VERGE OF LAW|THE 6-HOUR AMERICAN WORKDAY|green

shots.sub: Then came a wave of corporate lobbying.
Business leaders warned President Roosevelt that
if workers tasted 30 hours a week,
shots.spec: scene:27_lobby_hallway_top_hat.png+bubble:960,160,IF THEY TASTE 30 HRS, THEY'LL NEVER GO BACK!

shots.sub: they would never go back.
The bill was buried in the house.
Five years later, in 1938,
shots.spec: stamp:1938 • FLSA ACT|FAIR LABOR STANDARDS ACT|COUNTER LOCKED AT 40 HOURS|gold

shots.sub: the Fair Labor Standards Act locked the counter at 40 hours across five days.
And then the clock simply froze.
Since 1938, the productivity of an American
worker has increased by over 300 percent.
shots.spec: stamp:+300% PRODUCTIVITY|SINCE 1938|4X OUTPUT PER WORKER • SAME 40 HOURS|green

shots.sub: A task that took a room of clerks a
week in 1940 now takes a spreadsheet four seconds.
shots.spec: split:1940 CLERKS|1 FULL WEEK|ROOM OF PAPER LEDGERS ✕|red|TODAY'S LAPTOP|4 SECONDS|1 SPREADSHEET FORMULA ✓|green

shots.sub: By every law of math, Keynes should have been right.
We should be leaving our desks on Tuesday afternoon.
So why are you still sitting
shots.spec: clock:5|5:01 PM|FRIDAY • STILL AT YOUR DESK||1

shots.sub: there at 501 on a Friday?
shots.spec: scene:07_office_501pm_email_meeting.png+badge:FRIDAY 5:01 PM: WHY ARE YOU STILL HERE?|red

shots.sub: In 1955, historian Cyril Northcoat Parkinson
shots.spec: stamp:1955 • THE ECONOMIST|C. NORTHCOTE PARKINSON|THE SECRET OF MODERN OFFICE TIME|gold

shots.sub: wrote a famous line in The Economist.
Work expands so as to fill
shots.spec: stamp:PARKINSON'S LAW|WORK EXPANDS TO FILL|THE TIME AVAILABLE FOR ITS COMPLETION|red

shots.sub: the time available for its completion.
When society moved from factory floors to office desks,
shots.spec: split:FACTORY FLOOR|PHYSICAL OUTPUT|COUNT THE CARS & SHOES|gold|OFFICE DESK|CHAIR WARMTH|COUNT THE 40 HOURS ✕|red

shots.sub: we stopped measuring work by what you produce and kept
measuring it by how many days your chair is warm.
If a five-hour task is given 40 hours of office time,
it grows meetings, reports,
and email chains until it takes all 40 hours.
Anthropologist David Graber found that millions of
shots.spec: stamp:DAVID GRAEBER|ANTHROPOLOGIST STUDY|MILLIONS OF OFFICE WORKERS CONFESS|gold

shots.sub: office workers admit they could finish their
real work in 15 to 20 hours a week.
shots.spec: stamp:15 TO 20 HOURS|REAL WEEKLY WORK|THE OTHER 20+ HOURS IS THEATRE|green

shots.sub: Almost the exact same 17
hours recorded among Kalahari hunter -gatherers.
shots.spec: split:KALAHARI TRIBE|17 HRS / WK|HUNT, GATHER & REST ✓|green|REAL OFFICE WORK|15-20 HRS|PLUS 20H FAKE BUSYNESS ✕|red

shots.sub: The rest of the week is
spent performing the ritual of being busy.
And the extra welfare machines created?
Instead of trading it for Tuesday and Wednesday off,
shots.spec: scene:49_keynes_road_fork.png+x_slam:DID NOT TRADE IT FOR TUE & WED OFF ✕

shots.sub: our economy taught us to trade it for bigger houses,
newer phones, and faster subscriptions.
Things that require five days of paycheck to maintain.
The five-day work week is not an ancient human law.
It is barely
90 years old.
shots.spec: stamp:BARELY 90 YEARS OLD|1938 TO TODAY|A TINY BLIP IN HUMAN HISTORY|gold

shots.sub: It was born from steam engines,
polished by a carmaker who needed weekend shoppers,
shots.spec: scene:05_ford_1926_model_t_shopping.png+badge:2. POLISHED BY FORD FOR WEEKEND SHOPPERS|gold

shots.sub: and frozen in 1938.
Which makes that tightness in your
chest on Sunday night look very different.
shots.spec: scene:13_sunday_night_moon_sofa.png+badge:THAT SUNDAY NIGHT TIGHTNESS IN YOUR CHEST...|gold

shots.sub: Your body isn't broken for
dreading a 40 -hour fluorescent box.
Your body is just remembering
how human time used to work.
shots.spec: scene:32_twilight_sofa_peaceful_smile.png+badge:REMEMBERING HOW HUMAN TIME USED TO WORK.|green
